title: Ovarian Cancer: Persistent Nonspecific Symptoms Need a Pelvic Differential
bottomLine: Ovarian cancer has no effective population screening test for average-risk asymptomatic patients. Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary change, ascites or an adnexal mass require diagnostic evaluation, while hereditary-risk families need genetics/specialty pathways rather than CA-125 screening alone.
recognize: Symptoms are often nonspecific but concerning when new, persistent and frequent, especially after menopause.
Ascites, fixed/complex adnexal mass, weight loss or pleural effusion increases malignancy concern.
differentiate: Benign cysts, fibroids, GI disease and functional bloating can mimic symptoms; CA-125 can rise in many benign conditions.
assessment: Assess symptom duration/frequency, menopausal status, family history of ovarian/breast/colon cancer, prior BRCA/Lynch risk, exam for mass/ascites and GI/urinary alternatives.
workup: Use transvaginal/pelvic imaging and tumor markers only within a diagnostic risk-assessment pathway; do not use CA-125 alone to screen average-risk asymptomatic patients.
Refer suspicious masses to gynecologic oncology before non-oncologic surgery when possible.
management: Urgently refer high-risk adnexal masses/ascites/possible metastatic disease; stabilize obstruction, thrombosis or major effusion complications.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated empiric hormonal or GI treatment when persistent alarm symptoms or a suspicious mass requires diagnosis.
counselling: Explain that there is no routine ovarian cancer screen for average-risk people and symptoms, not screening tests, drive evaluation.
followUp: Track imaging, tumor-marker interpretation and oncology referral to definitive diagnosis.
examTrap: Ordering CA-125 as a screening test in an asymptomatic average-risk patient or dismissing persistent postmenopausal bloating as IBS without pelvic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Ovarian cancer is a symptom-and-mass diagnostic problem, not a CA-125 screening problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian gynecologic oncology/provincial ovarian cancer pathways

title: Vaginitis: Diagnose the Cause Before Treating the Discharge
bottomLine: Vaginal discharge/itch/odor has multiple causes—bacterial vaginosis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, trichomoniasis, cervicitis, GSM and noninfectious dermatitis. Use history, examination and point-of-care/lab testing as appropriate rather than treating every discharge empirically as yeast.
recognize: BV, candidiasis and trichomoniasis have overlapping symptoms and self-diagnosis is unreliable.
Postmenopausal GSM can cause dryness, burning, dyspareunia and recurrent urinary/vaginal symptoms without infection.
differentiate: Cervicitis/PID requires STI-focused assessment; vulvar dermatoses and irritant/contact disease can mimic infection.
assessment: Ask discharge/odor/itch/pain, sexual/STI risk, pregnancy, antibiotics/diabetes, products/irritants, menopause and prior confirmed episodes.
workup: Use vaginal pH/microscopy/NAAT or culture according to syndrome and availability; test for trichomonas/STIs when exposure or cervicitis risk exists.
management: Treat the confirmed/most likely cause with current Canadian/PHAC guidance and address recurrent disease risk factors.
Use vaginal estrogen or nonhormonal GSM therapy when appropriate after contraindication review.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy changes medication choices; repeated azole exposure without confirmation can delay another diagnosis.
counselling: Avoid stigma and explain that BV/yeast are not equivalent to an STI; partner treatment depends on the specific diagnosis.
followUp: Reassess recurrent/refractory symptoms and verify the diagnosis rather than automatically repeating the same treatment.
examTrap: Treating every itchy discharge as Candida without checking for BV, trichomonas, cervicitis or dermatitis.
oneLinePearl: Discharge is a symptom; the vaginal diagnosis determines the treatment.

title: PID: Treat Early When the Clinical Syndrome Fits
bottomLine: PID is often a clinical diagnosis and delayed treatment increases infertility/ectopic/chronic-pain risk. In a patient at STI risk with pelvic/lower-abdominal pain and cervical/uterine/adnexal tenderness without a better cause, test appropriately and begin current empiric treatment rather than waiting for definitive imaging or NAAT results.
recognize: Cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness plus discharge/bleeding/fever can support PID; symptoms may be mild.
differentiate: Ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, torsion, ovarian cyst complication and UTI can mimic PID.
assessment: Assess pregnancy, pain severity, fever, vomiting, hemodynamics, sexual/STI exposure, contraception/IUC, allergy and ability to adhere/follow up.
workup: Pregnancy testing and gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT are core; add HIV/syphilis testing and ultrasound when abscess/torsion/alternative diagnosis is plausible.
A negative GC/CT test does not exclude PID.
management: Use current PHAC PID regimen and partner/public-health management as applicable; admit/escalate pregnancy, severe illness, tubo-ovarian abscess, inability to tolerate oral therapy or diagnostic uncertainty requiring acute care.
medicationSafety: Do not remove an IUC automatically at PID diagnosis; manage according to current guidance and clinical response.
Review pregnancy/allergy/drug interaction before regimen selection.
counselling: Discuss STI prevention, partner treatment/testing and fertility implications without blame.
followUp: Reassess clinical improvement within the recommended short interval and escalate nonresponse.
examTrap: Waiting for positive chlamydia/gonorrhea testing before treating a convincing PID syndrome.
oneLinePearl: PID is treated on clinical probability because delay causes reproductive harm.
sourceBasis: PHAC Pelvic Inflammatory Disease Guide current 2026

title: STI Management: Test the Exposed Sites, Treat Current Guidance, Close the Partner Loop
system: Women's Health / Sexual Health / Public Health
bottomLine: STI care is anatomy/exposure-specific, current-guideline driven and partner/public-health aware. Test all exposed sites when indicated, use the current PHAC regimen rather than memorized old doses, evaluate complications and integrate HIV prevention, pregnancy and vaccination needs.
recognize: GC/CT and other STIs can be asymptomatic; pharyngeal/rectal infection is missed when testing follows gender assumptions rather than sexual exposure.
differentiate: Cervicitis/urethritis, PID, epididymitis, disseminated gonococcal disease and syphilis stages require different management.
assessment: Use inclusive sexual history covering practices/sites, symptoms, pregnancy, prior STI, antibiotics, allergies, partner status and HIV prevention needs.
workup: Use NAAT/culture/serology matched to infection and exposed sites; gonorrhea culture/test-of-cure follows current PHAC 2026 indications.
management: Treat according to current PHAC STBBI guides, manage partners and report when required; offer PrEP/PEP/HPV/hepatitis vaccination where relevant.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy and allergy change selected regimens; avoid obsolete gonorrhea therapy as national resistance guidance evolves.
counselling: Use nonstigmatizing partner/abstinence/barrier counselling and explain site-specific testing.
followUp: Complete test-of-cure/retesting and partner/public-health actions according to the infection.
examTrap: Testing only urine/cervix after oral/anal exposure or using an old memorized gonorrhea regimen.
oneLinePearl: STI testing follows exposure anatomy; treatment follows today's PHAC guidance.
sourceBasis: PHAC STBBI Guides including June 2026 gonorrhea updates

title: UTI in Women: Cystitis, Pyelonephritis, Pregnancy, or Not a UTI?
bottomLine: Acute uncomplicated cystitis is usually a symptom-based diagnosis in the right patient; fever/flank pain/systemic illness, pregnancy, obstruction or recurrent/atypical disease changes testing and treatment. Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria except in established indications such as pregnancy or selected urologic procedures.
recognize: Dysuria/frequency/urgency without vaginal symptoms supports cystitis; fever/flank pain/CVA tenderness raises pyelonephritis.
differentiate: Vaginitis/cervicitis/STI, urethral syndrome and GSM can mimic dysuria.
assessment: Assess pregnancy, fever/systemic symptoms, flank pain, vaginal/STI symptoms, prior resistant cultures, stones/obstruction, renal function and recurrence pattern.
workup: Urine culture is especially important in pyelonephritis, pregnancy, recurrent/complicated infection or treatment failure; routine culture may be unnecessary in classic uncomplicated cystitis.
management: Use current local Canadian empiric therapy based on syndrome/resistance and culture when indicated; pyelonephritis with sepsis, pregnancy complications or oral-treatment failure needs escalation.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic choice depends on pregnancy, renal function, allergies and local resistance; avoid fluoroquinolones/long courses when narrower evidence-based options are suitable.
counselling: Explain recurrence prevention and why positive urine results without symptoms often do not need antibiotics.
followUp: Review cultures for complicated cases and investigate recurrent atypical infection when indicated.
examTrap: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in a nonpregnant patient or calling dysuria with vaginal discharge a straightforward cystitis without another differential.
oneLinePearl: UTI treatment begins by naming the syndrome and deciding whether the patient is complicated.

title: Pelvic Floor Disorders: Prolapse, Incontinence, Emptying, and Function
bottomLine: Pelvic-floor symptoms are functional syndromes—pressure/bulge, stress or urgency incontinence, incomplete emptying, bowel dysfunction and sexual pain may coexist. Identify the dominant problem, assess retention and tissue/neurologic contributors, then use pelvic-floor therapy, pessary/behavioural/medical or surgical referral based on goals.
recognize: A vaginal bulge/pressure suggests prolapse; stress leakage differs from urgency incontinence; elevated residual urine suggests voiding dysfunction/overflow.
differentiate: Pelvic mass, severe constipation, neurologic disease, UTI and GSM can mimic or worsen pelvic-floor symptoms.
assessment: Assess obstetric/surgical history, urinary/bowel symptoms, sexual function, prolapse sensation, neurologic symptoms, medications and functional goals; perform pelvic exam when relevant/consented.
workup: Urinalysis and post-void residual are selective tools; urodynamics/imaging are not routine for every uncomplicated presentation.
management: Use pelvic-floor physiotherapy, bladder/bowel strategies, pessary or medication for appropriate syndromes; refer bothersome advanced prolapse, retention or refractory symptoms to urogynecology/urology.
medicationSafety: Antimuscarinics can worsen retention/constipation/cognitive burden; review before prescribing urgency therapy.
counselling: Normalize discussion and focus treatment on symptoms/function rather than prolapse stage alone.
followUp: Reassess residual/retention risk, pessary care and functional response.
examTrap: Ordering urodynamics before basic history/exam or treating urgency medication in a patient with significant retention.
oneLinePearl: Pelvic-floor care starts by identifying which function—support, storage, emptying, bowel or pain—is failing.

title: Sexual Dysfunction: Desire, Arousal, Orgasm, Pain, Context, and Safety
bottomLine: Sexual dysfunction is diagnosed from distressing problems with desire, arousal, orgasm or pain in biopsychosocial context. Ask permission, assess relationship/safety/medication/hormonal/pelvic factors and treat the dominant contributors rather than assuming low desire is a hormone deficiency.
recognize: SSRIs, pain, pelvic-floor dysfunction, GSM, postpartum changes, depression/anxiety, relationship factors and chronic disease can contribute.
differentiate: Pain disorders and GSM require local/pelvic evaluation; reproductive coercion/IPV can present as sexual distress and must not be medicalized as libido disorder.
assessment: Ask what changed, distress/goal, pain, lubrication/arousal/orgasm, relationship context, medications, menopause/postpartum, mood, trauma and safety using consent-based language.
workup: Testing is targeted to suspected endocrine/medical contributors; routine broad sex-hormone panels are not indicated for every complaint.
management: Treat contributing medication, pain, GSM, pelvic-floor, mood and relationship factors; use sex therapy/pelvic-floor therapy and evidence-based medication only for an appropriate diagnosis.
medicationSafety: Testosterone/systemic hormone therapy should not be prescribed solely from a low lab result without a validated indication and monitoring plan.
counselling: Normalize variability and center consent, pleasure, patient goals and autonomy rather than a performance standard.
followUp: Track distress/function and adverse effects; revise the diagnosis when treatment of one factor does not resolve the problem.
examTrap: Ordering a testosterone level and treating it as the explanation for all low desire without assessing medication, pain, mood or relationship safety.
oneLinePearl: Sexual function is biopsychosocial; the patient's distress and goals define what needs treatment.

title: Intimate Partner Violence: Ask Safely, Validate, Assess Immediate Danger, Preserve Autonomy
bottomLine: IPV care prioritizes privacy, trauma-informed inquiry, validation and immediate safety assessment. Do not pressure disclosure or force separation; identify high-risk violence, strangulation, weapons, escalating threats, reproductive coercion and child/dependent safety, then offer resources and document carefully within provincial reporting/privacy law.
recognize: IPV can include physical, sexual, psychological, financial, digital and reproductive control; pregnancy and separation can increase danger.
differentiate: Routine relationship conflict is not equivalent to coercive control/violence; sexual assault requires its own time-sensitive medical/forensic choices.
assessment: Ask privately without partner/family present, use professional interpreters, assess immediate danger, strangulation, weapons, homicide/suicide threats, children/dependents, pregnancy and safe methods of contact.
workup: Use injury/pregnancy/STI/strangulation evaluation according to exposure and symptoms; document objective findings and patient words accurately.
management: Address emergency injury/danger, offer advocacy/shelter/legal/social resources and develop a patient-led safety plan.
Follow provincial mandatory-reporting requirements for children/dependents or other legally defined circumstances; adult IPV disclosure alone does not automatically remove patient autonomy.
medicationSafety: Consider partner control of medications/contraception and safe dispensing/storage when relevant.
counselling: Validate without blame and avoid advice that could increase danger, such as confronting the partner or leaving without safety planning.
followUp: Offer discreet follow-up and verify safe communication/document access preferences.
examTrap: Insisting a competent adult leave immediately or contacting the partner to verify the story.
oneLinePearl: IPV care is safety plus autonomy—not forced disclosure or forced leaving.
sourceBasis: SOGC trauma- and violence-informed care resources
